messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Nuts and bananas
parts:
I am continuing evaluations, and am now looking at banana functions as described by Haario 1999.

They are useful because there are analytical solutions, but I have also changed them because they had most of the parameters with a diagonal variance of 1.0, which would be too favourable to many algorithms. I have instead made pairs of parameters have the same behaviour as the first two - much more difficult. Ideally I want to generalise further.

Also you can vary the amount of bananicity.

NUTS looks remarkably good, I will need to sleep on the issue of global v local Hessian approximations.

Zhang and Sutton HMCBFGS have some example code for Rosenbrock, but it doesn't appear they have tried the Haario function, nor has RHMCMC as far as I know.

My difficulty with the Rosenbrock tests is that there is no analytical solution, so I can't compare methods easily.

All of that sounds interesting, I'll be interested to hear more as it develops.

It's not obvious how to do RMHMC on a banana-shaped distribution,
since it's not log-concave and therefore you can't just use the
negative Hessian as (part of) a Riemannian metric. Which is a shame,
since it's precisely the sort of problem where local curvature
information would be most useful!

Matt

messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nuts and bananas
parts:
Yes, it's as though we need many Hessians - a global one, and one to go with each chain.

I've often thought the same when looking at population based heuristic optimisation methods - e.g. particle swarm keeps a momentum with each member of the population, so why not also keep a hessian with each member.

Thoughts for the day

- quasi newton methods in optimisation are used in conjunction with line searches and trust regions. The search avoids going off into the unknown when the hessian is poor, and trust regions restrict one to regions where the hessian is not changing too much.

- there is a whole heap of difference between quasi newton methods taught at school or in matlab demos versus the robust code developed by the experts like Powell, which have all kinds of checks. See for example links to robust code for unconsrained optimisation with derivatives on http://plato.asu.edu/sub/nlounres.html

- the method I use to control the positive definiteness of the hessian is to check the relative reduction in diagonal elements during cholesky factorisation.

- I also check changes in determinant after update.

- in NUTS, if the hessian is not positive definite enough, then epsilon becomes small and the number of leap frog steps increases

- the NUTS epsilon is equivalent to the optimisation trust region in a vague way.

So....I should really check the value of epsilon, and alter my criteria for positive definiteness dependent on epsilon. If epsilon is very low, make the hessian more positive.

Also, make better use of ideas from robust optimisation code.

messages.author: ace57905b77e39eb
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Nuts and bananas
parts:
This may be completely obvious to everybody, but worth noting.

In all cases I compare methods with roughly the same number of function evaluations.

For a high dimension multivariate highly correlated norm, DREAM does well and BFGS does well. Because the Hessian is fixed, and because DREAM likes points along a line.

So NUTS+DREAM+BFGS does very well, much better than NUTS alone.

However, for a banana function:

RW does better than DREAM (which makes sense, taking differences between two points at extremes of banana doesn't help the point in the middle much).

NUTS+DREAM+BFGS with a global Hessian (same for all chains) is not as good as NUTS alone. This is because DREAM does not work well, and the global Hessian is not so useful for a banana.

NUTS+RWM+BFGS with a local Hessian (one per chain) seems to work better, because RWM is better than DREAM and because the Hessian is more local.

I need to check out and implement the Goodman and Weare approach, and consider whether it can overcome limitations in DREAM for bananas.

DREAM does of course have some attraction in multi mode and discrete/integer situations, but maybe is too focussed on exploration rather than exploitation.

I don;t think I've seen a comparison between DREAM and Goodman and Weare.
